However, most airborne surveillance lasers and some LIDARs exceed the \nallowable class I AELs for the invisible wavelengths and therefore require variances as \ndescribed in § 1010.4. For products labeled under the classification system of the IEC, \nclasses 1, 2, and 3R are acceptable class limits for an invisible emission and therefore \ndo not require a variance. The FDA variance may require administrative controls \n(for example, the laser equipment purchasing organization is to maintain an active \nprogram of training for its employees in the safe use of the laser system) and technical \ncontrols (such as a range finder cutoff that disables the laser when the distance between \nthe laser’s aperture and the object being exposed is less than the NOHD).\n7.3 Aircraft Laser Equipment Installation.\n7.3.1 System Safety Analysis.\nYou must perform a system safety analysis to assess whether the installed laser \nequipment meets 14 CFR 23.1309, 25.1309, 27.1309, or 29.1309. Refer to \nAC 23.1309-1, System Safety Analysis and Assessment for Part 23 Airplanes. For \npart 25 airplanes, refer to AC 25.1309-1, System Design and Analysis. For part 27 \nrotorcraft, refer to AC 27.1309, Equipment, Systems and Installations. For part 29\n\nrotorcraft, refer to AC 29.1309, Equipment, Systems and Installations. The systems \nsafety assessment should address the following:\n7.3.1.1 Laser Equipment Malfunction.\nLaser equipment malfunction resulting in an aircraft crewmember’s or \npassenger’s eye or skin being exposed to invisible laser radiation \nexceeding the MPE is considered no less than a hazardous functional \nfailure condition and could be catastrophic if continued safe flight is not \npossible because of the severity of the laser damage to a pilot’s eye or \nskin. In your system safety assessment, you should document the rationale \nfor a hazardous functional failure condition classification. If there is no \ndirect or reflected path into the cockpit or cabin because of the location of \nthe laser and physical shielding provided by the aircraft structure, this \nfailure condition does not apply. \n7.3.1.2 System Safety Considerations.\nIn assessing the failure conditions, you should consider direct and \nreflected radiation; the location of the laser, laser beam steering \nmechanism, and circuitry; the use of mechanical, software, or airborne \nelectronic hardware (AEH) stops that prevent the laser from being steered \nin a direction that could result in the aircraft occupants’ eyes being \nexposed to direct or reflected radiation; laser arming and firing circuitry; \nand other design features whose malfunction could contribute to an \ninadvertent exposure or an exposure that exceeds the MPE (such as failure \nof the internal laser diffuser used to reduce the AEL). If the laser’s\nsteering stops are implemented in software or AEH, their assurance level \nshould be commensurate with the functional failure condition associated \nwith the stops. The polar region environment is defined as the area beginning at 5º to 30º \nlatitude from the pole, depending on location, and extending to either the north or south pole. \nAnomalies with the earth’s magnetic field in the polar region can provide erroneous magnetic heading \nindications. Aircraft will typically use true heading information when flying in Polar Regions. \n5.1.1 If the AHRS article is installed on aircraft intended to operate in the Polar Regions, the \napplicant should conduct a flight test demonstration to show proper operation for new AHRS articles \nor show previous successful flight test demonstration in an aircraft of like or similar installation. If the \nAHRS article was flight tested under the combined TSO-STC process, then the applicant should \nensure the aircraft complies with the TSO article installation limitations and STC.
